paragraphs: It was the White Rabbit, trotting slowly back and looking anxiously around as if it had lost something. She heard it muttering to itself, “The Duchess! The Duchess! Oh, my dear paws! Oh, my fur and whiskers! She’ll have me executed, as sure as ferrets are ferrets! Where can I have dropped them, I wonder?” Alice guessed at once that it was looking for the fan and the pair of white kid gloves, and she good-naturedly began searching for them, but they were nowhere to be found. Everything seemed to have changed since her swim in the pool, and the great hall, with the glass table and the little door, had vanished completely.

Very soon the Rabbit noticed Alice searching around and called out to her in an angry tone, “Why, Mary Ann, what are you doing out here? Run home this minute and fetch me a pair of gloves and a fan! Quick, now!” Alice was so frightened that she ran off at once in the direction it pointed, without trying to explain its mistake.

“He took me for his housemaid,” she said to herself as she ran. “How surprised he’ll be when he finds out who I am! But I’d better take him his fan and gloves, if I can find them.” As she said this, she came upon a neat little house with a bright brass plate on the door engraved with the name “W. RABBIT.” She went in without knocking and hurried upstairs, terrified that she might meet the real Mary Ann and be thrown out of the house before she had found the fan and gloves.

“How strange it seems,” Alice said to herself, “to be running errands for a rabbit! I suppose Dinah will be sending me on errands next!” And she began to imagine how that would go: “‘Miss Alice! Come here right now and get ready for your walk!’ ‘Coming in a minute, nurse! But I have to make sure the mouse doesn’t get out.’ Only I don’t think,” Alice went on, “they’d let Dinah stay in the house if she started ordering people around like that!”

By this time she had found her way into a tidy little room with a table by the window, and on it (as she had hoped) a fan and two or three pairs of tiny white kid gloves. She picked up the fan and a pair of gloves and was about to leave the room when her eye fell on a little bottle standing near the mirror. There was no label this time saying “DRINK ME,” but she uncorked it anyway and put it to her lips. “I know something interesting is bound to happen,” she said to herself, “whenever I eat or drink anything, so I’ll just see what this bottle does. I do hope it makes me grow large again, because I’m really tired of being such a tiny little thing!”

It did, and much sooner than she expected. Before she had drunk even half the bottle, she found her head pressing against the ceiling and had to stoop to keep from breaking her neck. She hastily put the bottle down, saying to herself, “That’s quite enough. I hope I don’t grow any more. As it is, I can’t get out of the door. I really wish I hadn’t drunk so much!”

Alas, it was too late for wishing! She kept on growing and growing, and very soon had to kneel on the floor. A minute later there wasn’t even room for that, so she tried lying down with one elbow against the door and the other arm curled around her head. Still she kept growing, and as a last resort she put one arm out of the window and one foot up the chimney, and said to herself, “Now I can’t do any more, whatever happens. What will become of me?”

Luckily for Alice, the little magic bottle had now had its full effect and she grew no larger. Still, it was very uncomfortable, and since there seemed no chance of her ever getting out of the room again, no wonder she felt unhappy.

“It was much nicer at home,” thought poor Alice, “when you weren’t always growing bigger and smaller and being ordered around by mice and rabbits. I almost wish I hadn’t gone down that rabbit hole. And yet, and yet, it’s rather curious, you know, this sort of life! I do wonder what can have happened to me! When I used to read fairy tales, I imagined that kind of thing never happened, and now here I am in the middle of one! There ought to be a book written about me, there really ought! And when I grow up, I’ll write one. But I’m grown up now,” she added sadly. “At least there’s no room to grow up any more in here.”

“But then,” thought Alice, “will I never get any older than I am now? That would be a comfort in one way: never being an old woman. But then, always having lessons to learn! Oh, I wouldn’t like that!”
“Oh, you silly Alice!” she answered herself. “How can you learn lessons in here? Why, there’s hardly room for you, and no room at all for any schoolbooks!”
And so she went on, taking first one side and then the other, and making quite a conversation of it. But after a few minutes she heard a voice outside and stopped to listen.

“Mary Ann! Mary Ann!” said the voice. “Fetch me my gloves this minute!” Then came the pattering of little feet on the stairs. Alice knew it was the Rabbit coming to look for her, and she trembled until she shook the house, completely forgetting that she was now about a thousand times bigger than the Rabbit and had no reason to be afraid of it.

Soon the Rabbit came up to the door and tried to open it. But the door opened inward, and Alice’s elbow was pressed hard against it, so that attempt failed. Alice heard it say to itself, “Then I’ll go around and get in through the window.”

“No, you won’t!” thought Alice. She waited until she thought she heard the Rabbit just under the window, and then she suddenly spread out her hand and snatched at the air. She didn’t catch anything, but she heard a little shriek and a fall and a crash of breaking glass, from which she concluded that it might well have fallen into a cucumber frame or something of the sort.
Next came an angry voice, the Rabbit’s: “Pat! Pat! Where are you?” And then a voice she had never heard before: “Sure, I’m here! Digging for apples, your honor!”
“Digging for apples, indeed!” said the Rabbit angrily. “Here! Come and help me out of this!” (More sounds of breaking glass.)
“Now tell me, Pat, what’s that in the window?”
“Sure, it’s an arm, your honor!” (He pronounced it “arrum.”)
“An arm, you goose! Who ever saw one that size? Why, it fills the whole window!”
“Sure, it does, your honor. But it’s an arm all the same.”
“Well, it has no business being there. Go and take it away!”

There was a long silence after this, and Alice could only hear whispers now and then, such as “Sure, I don’t like it, your honor, not one bit!” and “Do as I tell you, you coward!” At last she spread out her hand again and made another snatch at the air. This time there were two little shrieks and more sounds of breaking glass. “How many cucumber frames there must be!” thought Alice. “I wonder what they’ll do next! As for pulling me out of the window, I only wish they could! I certainly don’t want to stay in here any longer!”

She waited for some time without hearing anything more. At last there came a rumbling of little cartwheels and the sound of many voices all talking at once. She made out the words: “Where’s the other ladder? Well, I only had to bring one. Bill’s got the other. Bill! Fetch it here, lad! Here, put them up at this corner. No, tie them together first. They don’t reach half high enough yet. Oh, they’ll do well enough, don’t be fussy. Here, Bill! Catch hold of this rope. Will the roof hold? Watch that loose slate. Oh, it’s coming down! Heads below!” (A loud crash.) “Now, who did that? It was Bill, I bet. Who’s going down the chimney? No, not me! You do it! I won’t, then! Bill has to go down. Here, Bill! The master says you have to go down the chimney!”

“Oh! So Bill has to come down the chimney, does he?” said Alice to herself. “Wow, they seem to put everything on Bill! I wouldn’t be in Bill’s place for anything. This fireplace is narrow, to be sure, but I think I can kick a little!”

She drew her foot as far down the chimney as she could and waited until she heard a little animal (she couldn’t guess what kind) scratching and scrambling about in the chimney right above her. Then, saying to herself, “This is Bill,” she gave one sharp kick and waited to see what would happen next.

The first thing she heard was a general chorus of “There goes Bill!” Then the Rabbit’s voice alone: “Catch him, you by the hedge!” Then silence, and then another confusion of voices. “Hold up his head. Brandy now. Don’t choke him. How was it, old fellow? What happened to you? Tell us all about it!”

Last came a feeble, squeaky little voice (“That’s Bill,” thought Alice): “Well, I hardly know. No more, thank you, I’m better now. But I’m much too flustered to tell you. All I know is, something comes at me like a jack-in-the-box, and up I go like a rocket!”
“So you did, old fellow!” said the others.
“We must burn the house down!” said the Rabbit’s voice. And Alice called out as loud as she could, “If you do, I’ll set Dinah on you!”

There was instant dead silence, and Alice thought to herself, “I wonder what they’ll do next! If they had any sense, they’d take the roof off.” After a minute or two they began moving around again, and Alice heard the Rabbit say, “A wheelbarrow-load will do, to begin with.”

“A wheelbarrow-load of what?” thought Alice. But she didn’t have long to wonder, because the next moment a shower of little pebbles came rattling in at the window, and some of them hit her in the face. “I’ll put a stop to this,” she said to herself, and shouted, “You’d better not do that again!” which produced another dead silence.

Alice noticed, with some surprise, that the pebbles were all turning into little cakes as they lay on the floor, and a bright idea came to her. “If I eat one of these cakes,” she thought, “it’s sure to change my size. And since it can’t possibly make me bigger, it must make me smaller, I suppose.”

So she swallowed one of the cakes and was delighted to find that she began shrinking at once. As soon as she was small enough to get through the door, she ran out of the house and found quite a crowd of little animals and birds waiting outside. Poor little Bill the Lizard was in the middle, being held up by two guinea pigs, who were giving him something out of a bottle. They all rushed at Alice the moment she appeared, but she ran off as fast as she could and soon found herself safe in a thick wood.

“The first thing I have to do,” Alice said to herself as she wandered through the wood, “is grow to my right size again, and the second thing is to find my way into that lovely garden. I think that’s the best plan.”

It sounded like an excellent plan, no doubt, and very neatly and simply put. The only difficulty was that she had no idea how to go about it. While she was peering anxiously among the trees, a sharp little bark just over her head made her look up in a hurry.

An enormous puppy was looking down at her with huge round eyes and feebly stretching out one paw, trying to touch her. “Poor little thing!” said Alice in a coaxing tone, and she tried hard to whistle to it. But she was terribly afraid the whole time that it might be hungry, in which case it would very likely eat her up in spite of all her coaxing.

Hardly knowing what she was doing, she picked up a little bit of stick and held it out to the puppy. The puppy jumped into the air with all four feet at once, yelping with delight, and rushed at the stick and pretended to wrestle with it. Alice dodged behind a big thistle to keep from being run over, and the moment she appeared on the other side, the puppy made another rush at the stick and tumbled head over heels in its hurry to grab it. Then Alice, feeling that it was very like playing with a cart horse, and expecting at any moment to be trampled under its feet, ran around the thistle again. Then the puppy began a series of short charges at the stick, running a very little way forward each time and a long way back, barking hoarsely all the while, until at last it sat down a good distance away, panting, with its tongue hanging out of its mouth and its great eyes half shut.
This seemed to Alice a good chance to escape, so she set off at once and ran until she was quite tired and out of breath, and until the puppy’s bark sounded very faint in the distance.

“And yet what a dear little puppy it was!” said Alice, leaning against a buttercup to rest and fanning herself with one of its leaves. “I would have loved to teach it tricks, if only I’d been the right size to do it! Oh dear! I’d almost forgotten that I have to grow up again! Let me see, how can I manage it? I suppose I ought to eat or drink something. But the big question is, what?”

The big question certainly was, what? Alice looked all around her at the flowers and the blades of grass, but she didn’t see anything that looked like the right thing to eat or drink in the circumstances. There was a large mushroom growing near her, about the same height as she was. When she had looked under it, and on both sides of it, and behind it, it occurred to her that she might as well look and see what was on top of it.

She stretched up on tiptoe and peeped over the edge of the mushroom, and her eyes immediately met those of a large blue caterpillar, which was sitting on top with its arms folded, quietly smoking a long hookah and taking not the slightest notice of her or of anything else.
